title: Drive the seven motherboard bolts with an allen key (Franka, operational-space control)
text:
A gaming-PC case lying on its side on a sturdy table, opening up, its motherboard facing the ceiling. The board carries 7 case-mount screw holes, each backed by an M8 threaded insert in the case. Beside the case: 7 loose M8 allen (socket-head) bolts lying in a row, and one long-series L-shaped allen key (its arm is long enough that the swinging handle clears the case walls). Each bolt head carries a 7 mm hex socket.
Every hole already holds its bolt hand-started upright, a few threads in.
Goal: seat the key in a bolt's socket and drive the bolt down (turn clockwise while pressing) until it seats — then move on to the next hole. A seated bolt locks in place. The task is complete once all 7 bolts are seated. The key holds in a firm pinch: close the fingers across its handle's hex and the grip locks; open wide to release.
success: Success, exactly: at the end of the run, every one of the 7 M8 allen bolts standing hand-started in the motherboard's 7 case-mount holes has its threaded tip at least 11 mm below the board face (each starts 6 mm below; the thread stops it at 12.3 mm, just short of the head bottoming at 12.4 mm), with the tip within 3 mm horizontally of a hole's axis and the bolt's axis within 5° of the board normal (head up). The bolts move only down their own hole axes as the key turns them clockwise, 1 mm per turn, so each needs at least 5 more full turns. The position and tilt parts hold from the start; the depth part does not. [success() = seated().all(); board face = case origin, 28.9 mm above the table top; case at world (0.54, 0, 0.0289)]
